mcqs.question: In the LRU cache's node-removal step, why must the recency list be doubly linked rather than singly linked to keep it O(1)?
options: Removing a node needs its predecessor's `next` pointer; without a stored `prev` reference, finding that predecessor means scanning from the head, which is O(n)
A singly linked list cannot store more than one value per node
Doubly linked lists are inherently faster to iterate during an eviction sweep
The hashmap needs two pointers per entry to compute key hashes correctly
mcqs.explanation: Unlinking an arbitrary node requires rewriting both its predecessor's and successor's pointers. With only `next` pointers, you don't have direct access to the predecessor and must walk from the head to find it — O(n). A `prev` pointer on every node is what makes removal O(1) regardless of where the node sits in the list; it has nothing to do with node capacity, iteration speed, or hashing.

mcqs.question: An LRU cache uses a doubly linked list for recency, but on eviction it scans the whole list to find the node with the oldest access time. What's actually wrong with this implementation?
options: It isn't thread-safe by default
Eviction is O(n) because it searches for the least-recently-used node instead of trusting a tail pointer kept correct by move-to-front updates on every access
It requires a hashmap to function at all, which most LRU designs avoid
It cannot support a TTL alongside capacity-based eviction
mcqs.explanation: A doubly linked list only delivers O(1) eviction if the tail is *already* guaranteed to be the least-recently-used node, by moving touched nodes to the head on every access. Scanning to find the victim throws that guarantee away and makes eviction O(n) no matter how the list is wired. Thread-safety and TTL support are separate, unrelated concerns.

mcqs.question: Why can't a plain read-write lock let concurrent get() calls run the way it typically does for a read-heavy structure?
options: Read-write locks only work with array-backed structures, not linked lists
Concurrent reads are unsafe for any shared data structure, regardless of design
get() mutates the list by moving the accessed node to the head, so it behaves as a writer with respect to the list even though it only reads the stored value
The hashmap component cannot be read without holding an exclusive write lock
mcqs.explanation: A read-write lock helps only when reads are truly read-only. Here, every get() rewrites prev/next pointers to move the node to the front, so two concurrent gets under a shared read-lock can race on those pointers and corrupt the list. There's no structural reason read-write locks fail on linked lists generally, or that the hashmap specifically needs exclusive access.

mcqs.question: A key's TTL expires while it's still resident in the cache. What must the removal do to keep the map and list consistent?
options: Remove it from the hashmap only; the linked list will self-correct on the next eviction
Unlink it from the list only; the map entry can be cleaned up lazily on the next get
Mark the node as expired but leave both structures untouched until the next active sweep
Remove the node from the hashmap and unlink it from the list in the same operation
mcqs.explanation: A node is only valid if both structures agree it exists. Removing from just one leaves the other pointing at a node that's supposed to be gone — a dangling map entry, or a list node an eviction could still touch. Whichever path detects expiry (lazy check on access, or the active sweep) must remove from both together.

mcqs.question: Why might an interviewer favor LFU over LRU for a cache holding a small set of consistently 'hot' keys, despite LFU's extra bookkeeping?
options: LFU has strictly better time complexity for get() than LRU
LRU can evict a genuinely hot key just because a single burst of one-off scan traffic pushed it to the tail; LFU's frequency tracking resists that
LFU doesn't need a hashmap to achieve O(1) lookup
FIFO and LFU behave identically for hot-key workloads, so the choice doesn't matter
mcqs.explanation: LRU only knows recency, so a large one-time scan of cold keys pushes genuinely hot keys toward the tail and can evict them. LFU tracks how often a key is used, so a hot key with high frequency survives a scan that only touched each cold key once. LFU is still O(1) but needs a hashmap just like LRU; FIFO ignores access pattern entirely and is the worst fit of the three.
